Unless you're dealing with a ridiculous amount of traffic, I'd say as long as you stick to the popular distributions it isn't going to make too much of a difference what distro you use and it's a matter of personal preference. It used to be if you wanted to make web apps/sites that used a database, the standard was LAMP (linux, apache, mysql, php). I'd say php has fallen out of favor and there are better solutions available. I personally like django, a web framework. You write all your code in python. It abstracts the database stuff (you can use mysql or postgres) so you don't work with it directly. Consequently, it's not ideal for learning sql since all that stuff gets handled behind the scenes.

In terms of topics to cover, I'd suggest familiarizing yourself with shell utilities, regular expressions, how to string commands together. Get comfortable using vim. If you're moving into an existing production environment then you'll want to learn whatever languages that stuff uses but apart from that mysql and python would be good to know.

You should be able to look up beginnner's guides for any of that stuff but hopefully those topics are the kinds of thing you're after and you find any of this useful.

This is a pretty solid approach. You can swap out particular programs/distros, but do all this and you'll be ace. The best way to learn to be an admin is to get your hands dirty.

https://voat.co/v/linuxadmin/comments/255611

Also, CentOS/Red Hat are probably the most widely used distros for servers, but Ubuntu is making great inroads. Personally, I'm an Ubuntu admin, and I've been toying with CentOS, just for more exposure, since they are fairly different in the way they do things. 95% of it is all the same distro to distro though, so don't sweat it too much.

Instead of reading a book, or a website, just start moving out of your comfort zone and use the command line for almost every task.

As you come across topics you don't know about, do a search and there will probably be something posted somewhere on that topic. This way you are specifically learning the things you need to know and not wasting your time on a tutorial which is going to lead you down a rabbit hole.

As for the distro question. None / Any. Except, you might want to use the server version of a particular distro. For instance, if you are using Ubuntu for your desktop work, you might use Ubuntu Server for your Databases. Keep in mind you'll have to use another machine to do this. But it would be good practice for you to use a server apart from your work machine.

Of course, you can always just install the SQL server on your desktop. There really isn't much difference between a Desktop distro and a Server Distro. But it's bad form in my opinion.

Like Master_Foo says:

Get a cheap box 2 or 3 generations back. Install a distro and a LAMP stack. Build a little web app on this server using your regular workstation. Back it up. Redo your server with another distro or version. Restore your app. Solve the problems. Install django. Install Wordpress. Play around. Back your stuff up. Rinse and repeat. Learn from your restore problems when they don't really matter.

My current project is putting a backup server and a web server on an old box with 2G RAM. This is for my home network. And I'm retired. But you got to keep your hand in.

What distros are most useful in database/server operations

Any distro you are already familiar with. As long as you can have a core install (no graphical tools) then you're good to go. If you know ubuntu well, use ubuntu on your servers. It's no good being familiar with (eg;) ubuntu and whacking CentOS on your server.

Red Hat seems to be the gold standard for Linux server distros.

I would personally install and configure Gentoo, Arch Linux, or Parabola as a crash course in the configuration and maintenance of a Linux system. Get very comfortable with the command line (bash, specifically, as it's most common), as best practice is not to have a GUI on a server, as GUIs present more security loopholes. (The fewer packages, the better, basically).

You may also eventually want to try to install a minimalistic window manager like Fluxbox or Openbox so you can see what a really simple Linux GUI looks like.

Maybe learn either Django or Node.js to help with web development and such. SQLite might be a good place to start for SQL.

Oh, and IMHO, you should get comfortable with Vim or Emacs. (I don't think it matters which, but fans from both sides will probably talk your ear off about it. Also, use GNU Nano for text editing to get started.)

A bit of an unconventional answer from me: Give yourself one month time, put together some old hardware (or get new one, whatever you like) and set up a server that is hosting a GitLab site. This involves everything you ask for plus a big chunk of background knowledge.

  1. You may connect a screen to it, but only until you have set up OpenSSH securely.
  2. From there on, you will configure one web server or another
  3. Set up one database or another
  4. Deal with Unix user- and group-permissions to set up git
  5. And finally install, configure and get running your instance of GitLab

You don't have to be a programmer for any of that, and the setup can be of great use to you as a non-coder. Even though git is mostly used for code versioning, lots of people use it to version-control their dotfiles or any other text files really. And GitLab has really good issue tracking (including milestones), provides a useful project wiki, etc.

Going the extra mile might involve setting up a Tor hidden service to access your local GitLab server from anywhere outside your LAN through a secure channel. At that point you could also set up SSL/TLS for GitLab, creating your own certificates and learning more about public key crypto (after you have already used SSH).

You can use any distro you want, but if your goal is to learn as much as possible about Unix administration, I suggest either Arch Linux or Debian, but try to stick to the TTY. Good luck.
